Abstract
The improvement in blast fragmentation material size aids downstream operation efﬁciency by supplying a high
percentage of 80% passing size of rocks (D80) material. In this study, blast fragmentation percentage prediction
models were developed using ﬁve soft computing approaches, i.e., multilayer perceptron (MLP), multivariate
adaptive regression spline (MARS), support vector regression SVR), decision tree (DT), and random forest (RF),
combined with reptile search algorithm. Blast characteristics were obtained from 407 production blasts at the
Anguran lead and zinc mine in Mahenshan, Iran. The particle size distribution resulting from blasting was
determined using a digital image processing approach in the current paper. The novelty of this research lies in the
integration of the reptile search algorithm (RSA) with machine-learning models for enhanced rock fragmentation
prediction. In this study, the RSA was used to optimize RF model and accurate prediction of rock fragmentation
due to mine blasting. The proposed models’ prediction accuracy was compared using nine performance indices
such as root mean square error (RMSE), correlation coefﬁcient (R), coefﬁcient of determination (R2), mean
absolute percentage error (MAPE), weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE), Variance Accounted For
(VAF), Nash–Sutcliffe efﬁciency (NS), Willmott’s index of agreement (WI) and bias index (Bias). Based on the
obtained results, the RF-RSA model outperformed other developed models with the lowest error and highest
accuracy. Hence, the results indicated that the RF-RSA model outperforms other models in predicting blast
fragmentation, achieving the lowest R2 of 0.9734 and RMSE of 0.8386 in the training phase, and 0.9715 and
0.7464 in the testing phase. Furthermore, the model attained the lowest MAPE values of 2.3067 (training) and
2.0959 (testing), demonstrating its robustness and predictive accuracy. These ﬁndings highlight the effectiveness
of the proposed AI-based approach in optimizing blast fragmentation prediction, contributing to improved
operational efﬁciency in mining.

1 Introduction
Mining is the safe and technologically advanced extraction of rocks, minerals, and other geological elements from
the earth for economic and human advantage. These activities employ a variety of approaches to discover and
extract raw resources for industrial application [1]. The extraction process is capital-demanding and necessitates
good approaches and procedures to avoid excessive operation expenses during fragmentation and downstream
operations [2].
Blasting is the employment of a precise amount of explosive to fragment a rock mass [3]. The importance of
blasting should not be forgotten during rock extraction as the outcomes and costs of blasting have a signiﬁcant
impact on later operations such as loading, haulage, and beneﬁciation [4–6]. As may be seen, blasting serves a
multitude of objectives. On the one hand, optimizing fragment distribution has a positive impact on downstream
energy use. The mining industry has long been worried about how to control the particle size distribution of a
muck-pile after a blast. The effectiveness of all mining subsystems is dependent on size distribution, according to
a study conducted at Quebec Cartier Mines and mentioned by Enayatollahi [7].
Today, researchers argue for a ‘‘mine-to-mill’’ blasting strategy, which involves maximizing the blast design to
optimize total proﬁtability rather than the proﬁtability of individual activities. If the particles are all roughly
equivalent in size, secondary blasting of large rocks is unnecessary [8]. Blasting causes rock breakage, which is a
typical activity in mining and civil engineering that must be thoroughly investigated. It is best to consider the
factors required for adequate breaking to prevent disrupting the unexplained costs of loading, carrying, crushing,
and milling [9]. As a result, it is necessary to ﬁrst identify the parameters involved in the drilling and blasting
activities, as well as the rock mass attributes in which the primary operations are carried out. In other words,
monitoring the blast-generated fragment distribution size aids downstream operations in improving efﬁciency and
lowering costs throughout the production chain.
The results of this operation, such as muck-pile shape, breakage, dilution bulking, and rock microfracture,
reveal a considerable impact on the efﬁciency of downstream operations, including crushing and grinding, taking
into account environmental effects that could motivate a helpful size distribution determination [10], as illustrated
in Fig. 1a. Budgets and output have been studied in activities where mining is the primary transmission of the ore
deposit from one location to another. In addition, activity management is carried out in order to maximize
production while reducing overall mining costs [11], as shown in Fig. 1b. In general, the costs associated with
crushing and grinding constitute a reasonable portion of the total cost (40–60% of the total mine-grinding cost).
As a result, relocation of unit operations considerably contributes to increased efﬁciency and lower costs.
Prediction models, for example, can be used to estimate blast particle size distribution and enhance drilling and
blasting operations in order to optimize the size distribution of rock blasting. Nonetheless, as seen in Fig. 1c, this
could result in higher drilling and blasting costs [12].
Blast design variables are divided into two categories, i.e., controllable and uncontrollable parameters [13, 14].
First are the variables under control including the initiation sequence, explosives (typically ANFO), and blast
pattern design (burden, spacing, hole diameter, and so on). Uncontrollable variables involve the geo-mechanical
and geological characteristics of the rock mass. The approach of selecting the aforementioned factors is based on
specialized knowledge that enables the engineers to maximize the performance and efﬁciency of the succeeding
steps by taking advantage of the total energy of the explosive. Hence, a swarm-based metaheuristic algorithm
used in this study to identify trends between design parameters and particle size distributions. The novelty of the
proposed work lies in developing a novel predictive model using machine-learning techniques tailored to the
unique characteristics of the rock blasting process in mining operations. Unlike conventional models, this
approach integrates multiple machine-learning algorithms and optimization techniques to enhance the accuracy
and reliability of predictions. The signiﬁcance of this work is that it provides a robust framework for optimizing
rock blasting operations, which is critical for improving productivity and reducing environmental impacts in
mining projects. By offering a comprehensive understanding of the factors affecting blasting efﬁciency, our study
contributes to more sustainable and cost-effective mining practices.

2 Review of machine-learning application to blast fragmentation
Machine learning (ML) plays a crucial role in making mining operations more sustainable, productive, and safe.
A multitude of empirical and soft computing models that take into consideration historical blasting experience
and outputs can be used to estimate the size distribution of the blasted muck-pile [15]. The presence of big
fragments within blast fragmentation reduces productivity while also increasing the costs associated with loading
and subsequent operational processes. Several attempts have been made to improve blasting results by using
empirical models and machine-learning methods [16]. In recent years, artiﬁcial neural network modeling has
grown rapidly as a solution to a wide range of commercial and scientiﬁc problems. Akkem et al. [17] provided an
in-depth exploration of how artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) can address contemporary challenges. It emphasizes the
integration of machine learning, deep learning, and time series analysis in smart farming practices. The review
details the application of these AI techniques.
ML is a type of computer modeling that constructs a network structure from the interactions between two or
more variables. Several previous learning-based approaches are used to forecast variable distributions during
artiﬁcial neural network (ANN) model building, with subsequent weight and bias change. Despite its potential as
one of the most interesting biologically inspired computational intelligence technologies, building an ANN is a
challenging task due to the need to conﬁgure various sophisticated parameters to achieve the best possible weight
and bias.
Several models to predict rock blast-induced fragmentation have been developed. Hjelmberg [18] developed
the SveDeFo model for predicting rock fragment size using data such as rock mass blastability factor and blast
pattern parameters such as burden, spacing, stemming, blasthole depth and powder factor. To anticipate blast
fragmentation, the Kuznetsov-Cunningham-Ouchterlony model integrated blast design parameters, explosive
properties, and rock properties [19]. Roy and Dhar [20] exploited rock joint characteristics and orientation to
build their fragmentation model. The source of data used to construct current empirical models restricts their
usage. The model’s limitation is that it is inapplicable to diverse mining situations [21]. More importantly, access
to sufﬁcient parameters that span all rock kinds, mines, and countries is impossible, especially when time is
limited.
Different models for predicting rock blast-induced fragmentation have been developed. According to Bahrami
et al. [22], new imaginative and more powerful methods, such as those incorporating ML, are necessary to
anticipate rock fragmentation. Many academics have concentrated on fragmentation prediction using ML, ANN,
and fuzzy inference systems (FIS). Furthermore, several studies have focused on various methods, new models,
and hybrid models. Monjezi et al. [21] used multiple regression analysis (MRA) and FIS to anticipate fragment
size after blast rounds at the Gol-E-Gohar iron mine. They examined the prediction performance of both models,
and their results showed that the fuzzy model was more accurate. Monjezi et al. [23] created an ANN model to
forecast blast fragmentation (D80) at the Sangan iron mine. Their ﬁndings demonstrated that ANN may be utilized
efﬁciently to assess blasting efﬁciency. Bahrami et al. [22] also used ANN method to estimate rock size in the
Sangan iron mine. The ANN technique demonstrated good correlation in their investigation, indicating that the
method accurately predicts rock fragmentation. Sayadi et al. [24] used a dataset from Tehran Cement Company
limestone mines in Iran to construct fragmentation and backbreak prediction models utilizing a back propagation
neural network (BPNN) and radial basis function neural network (RBFNN). According to their ﬁndings, while
burden and stemming are the most effective criteria, the speciﬁc charge is the least effective.
Karami and Aﬁuni-Zadeh [25] estimated D80 at the Gol-E-Gohar iron mine in Sirjan, Iran, using ANFIS and
radial basis function (RBF) approaches. According to their ﬁndings, the RBF model is statistically acceptable,
while the ANFIS suggested model is superior and also simpler. The D80 was predicted for Iran’s Sarcheshmeh
copper mine using FIS and MRA [26]. Their comparison of ﬁndings indicated that the FIS model outperformed
the MRA model. Ebrahimi et al. (2016) assessed fragmentation and backbreak parameters for optimizing blast
design factors at the Anguran mine in Iran using the ANN and ABC algorithms. They claimed that the proposed
algorithm could optimize rock fragmentation with sufﬁcient precision. For fragmentation prediction, Hasanipanah

forests (RF), and decision trees (DT). To improve the ﬁve models’ performance as a tool for forecasting the
percentage blast D80 size material in blasting output, the paper also introduces a swarm-based metaheuristic
algorithm inspired by crocodile encirclement and hunt mechanisms reptile search algorithm (RSA). Based on the
best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst paper to use the cutting-edge RSA method to predict blast fragmentation.

3 Case study and data description
3.1 Description of case study area
Anguran lead and zinc mine is located in Mahenshan city and 135 km west of Zanjan city. The nearest village to
the mine is GhaleJouk village and the closest city to it is Dandi. The main access road has a distance of about
120 km. The difference in temperature during the day and night, as well as between the cold and hot seasons in
the mine site, is large. The reserves of Anguran mine are 8,000,000 tons (28.27% zinc and 4.39% lead) in the open
pit and four million tons in the underground part [34]. Taking into account the annual extraction of one million
tons of minerals, the remaining life of Anguran mine will end in 12 years. Anguran mine is one of the rare mines
in the world in terms of high-grade metal content. In the Anguran mine, the lead–zinc is extracted by blasting.
The main operations implemented in this mine to extract lead–zinc are drilling, blasting, loading, hauling, and
crushing [35]. Blasting rounds are operated by drilling holes with a length of 6.5–12.5 m (Fig. 2).
Measurement of rock size is slightly more difﬁcult. This research used a digital image processing approach to
specify the rock fragmentation resulting from blasting. This approach is preferable to the classic sieve method
owing to the fact that it is more accurate, quicker, and more cost-effective. A signiﬁcant number of digital photos
of the muck-pile were collected after a thorough analysis of the muck-pile. It should be emphasized that the rocks
on the muck-pile’s surface do not accurately depict the distribution of particle sizes [36]. As a result, images of
the rock size within the trucks and shovels bucket were also taken in order to determine the rock size distribution
with great accuracy. The fragmentation quality has been expressed by the 80% passing sizes of rock (D80). D80
affect the ﬁll factor for the shovel bucket negative effects. Acceptable ﬂeet efﬁciency is closely correlated to lower
D80. This parameter’s amount is one of the most crucial and essential criteria affecting the quality of haulage as
well as the effectiveness of crushing operations. In order to examine digital pictures gathered from blasted rocks
and determine particle size distributions, Split-Desktop version 4.0 was taken into consideration in this research.
In order to get a satisfactory outcome, a dataset including 407 blasting works is compiled.

challenges. MARS was utilized by Naser et al. [40] to construct a prediction model for the compressive strength
of eco-friendly concrete. Fu and Peng [41] used MARS modeling approaches to forecast the uniaxial compressive

5 Results and discussion
5.1 Model comparison
The models developed in the proposed study for the prediction of blast fragmentation 80% percentage using the
MLP, MARS, SVR, DT, and RF were compared with the models optimized with reptile search algorithms (MLP-
RSA, MARS-RSA, SVR-RSA, DT-RSA, and RF-RSA) (Fig. 19). In Fig. 19, the predictions of the suggested
models were compared to the predictions of the ﬁve non-optimized models. For the predicted 80% size per-
centage, the R2 values of the model developed with MLP, MARS, SVR, DT, and RF are 0.9421, 0.9273, 0.8797,
0.9254, and 0.9524 for the training dataset, respectively, while the R2 values of the RSA optimized models for
MLP-RSA, MARS-RSA, SVR-RSA, DT-RSA, and RF-RSA are 0.9523, 0.9473, 0.9051, 0.9389, and 0.9734,
respectively. The comparison reveals that optimized models are more accurate than proposed models. Most
notably, the RF-RSA model presents the most accurate prediction results for both the training and testing datasets.

6 Conclusions
When evaluating downstream operating efﬁciency, the impact of blast fragmentation size is indeed critical. D80 is
the fragment size that allows for 80% passage efﬁciency. Smaller blast fragment sizes minimize the amount of
energy and time required for crushing and grinding, boosting operational efﬁciency. Furthermore, blast products
with a high percentage of D80 size are easier to handle, load, and transport, lowering operational costs and
equipment needs. Understanding the amount of certain material size in blast fragmentation, such as D80, can help
downstream operation efﬁciency and offer information for loading operation planning.
This research shows that optimal artiﬁcial intelligence models outperform manually-adjusted ones in fore-
casting D80 material size in a blast outcome. Data was gathered in the blasting time of the Anguran mine near
Mahenshan, Iran, 135 km west of Zanjan. Blast parameters from 407 manufacturing blasts were gathered. The
particle size distribution resulting from blasting was determined by importing a digital image processing approach
in the Split-Desktop software.
According to the ﬁndings, the percentage of fragmentation D80 size passing through the crusher gape (PB-D80)
has a weak negative connection with B ( - 0.026), Pf (- 0.28), and CD (- 0.035). A negative correlation
suggests that one value rises while another falls. The burden also has a weak relationship with K (0.031), HA
(0.028), and St (0.22). For the construction of blast fragmentation prediction models, ﬁve prediction algorithms
(MARS, MLP, SVR, DT, and RF) were used. The RSA was used to optimize the optimum solution search rate for
MARS, MLP, SVR, DT, and RF machine learning and regression algorithms in order to increase their perfor-
mance. The ten models’ prediction accuracy was evaluated using RMSE, MAPE, NS, R, R2, MAE, VAF, WI,
WMAPE, and Bias metrics. As a consequence of the error analysis results, the RF-RSA soft computing model
was determined to be the best model for predicting blast fragment D80 size percentage. Looking ahead, future
research could beneﬁt from incorporating real-time data from blasting operations to dynamically reﬁne predic-
tions and adapt to changing conditions. Exploring advanced optimization algorithms beyond RSA can further
enhance model performance. Multi-objective optimization could balance fragmentation size with other opera-
tional parameters like cost and energy consumption. Additionally, including a broader set of input parameters,
such as geological and environmental factors, could improve model robustness. Field implementation and long-
term impact studies are also recommended to validate model applicability and assess their effects on operational
efﬁciency, equipment wear, and environmental impact.

Abstract: The improvement in blast fragmentation material size aids downstream operation efﬁciency by supplying a high percentage of 80% passing size of rocks (D80) material. In this study, blast fragmentation percentage prediction models were developed using ﬁve soft computing approaches, i.e., multilayer perceptron (MLP), multivariate adaptive regression spline (MARS), support vector regression SVR), decision tree (DT), and random forest (RF), combined with reptile search algorithm. Blast characteristics were obtained from 407 production blasts at the Anguran lead and zinc mine in Mahenshan, Iran. The particle size distribution resulting from blasting was determined using a digital image processing approach in the current paper. The novelty of this research lies in the integration of the reptile search algorithm (RSA) with machine-learning models for enhanced rock fragmentation prediction. In this study, the RSA was used to optimize RF model and accurate prediction of rock fragmentation due to mine blasting. The proposed models’ prediction accuracy was compared using nine performance indices such as root mean square error (RMSE), correlation coefﬁcient (R), coefﬁcient of determination (R2), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE), Variance Accounted For (VAF), Nash–Sutcliffe efﬁciency (NS), Willmott’s index of agreement (WI) and bias index (Bias). Based on the obtained results, the RF-RSA model outperformed other developed models with the lowest error and highest accuracy. Hence, the results indicated that the RF-RSA model outperforms other models in predicting blast fragmentation, achieving the lowest R2 of 0.9734 and RMSE of 0.8386 in the training phase, and 0.9715 and 0.7464 in the testing phase. Furthermore, the model attained the lowest MAPE values of 2.3067 (training) and 2.0959 (testing), demonstrating its robustness and predictive accuracy. These ﬁndings highlight the effectiveness of the proposed AI-based approach in optimizing blast fragmentation prediction, contributing to improved operational efﬁciency in mining.
